extracted.intended_audience: Authors submitting to NeurIPS (and members of program/organizing committees)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and submitting machine-learning research to NeurIPS in an ethically responsible way, covering human-subjects, data handling, societal impacts, mitigation measures, and legal/compliance expectations. Intended to inform authors and reviewers about required ethical practices and communication in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair Wages
rubrics_metrics.description: all human research subjects or participants must receive appropriate compensation. If you make use of crowdsourcing or contract work for a particular task as part of your research project, you must respect the minimum hourly rate in the region where the work is carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation should reflect local minimum hourly rates for crowdsourced or contracted workers; authors must ensure participants are paid fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-participant ethical review (IRB or equivalent)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the research presented involves direct interactions between the researchers and human participants or between a technical system and human participants, authors are required to follow existing protocols in their institutions (e.g. human subject research accreditation, IRB) and go through the relevant process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where no formal process exists, authors should undergo an equivalent informal process (e.g. via their peers or an internal ethics review) and document that review in submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy (dataset PII minimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should minimize the exposure of any personally identifiable information, unless informed consent from those individuals is provided to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid releasing or exposing PII in datasets; where PII is present, explicit consent is expected or justification must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent for datasets involving real people
rubrics_metrics.description: Any paper that chooses to create a dataset with real data of real people should ask for the explicit consent of participants, or explain why they were unable to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If explicit consent cannot be obtained, authors must explain and justify the absence of consent and describe mitigations taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deprecated datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should take care to confirm with dataset creators that a dataset is still available for use. Datasets taken down by the original author (ie. deemed obsolete, or otherwise discontinued), should no longer be used, unless it is for the purposes of audit or critical assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check dataset availability and authorship permission; avoid using datasets removed by their creators except for clear audit/critique purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright and fair use compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: While the norms of fair use and copyright in machine learning research are still evolving, authors must respect the terms of datasets that have defined licenses (e.g. CC 4.0, MIT, etc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm and follow dataset and code licenses when using or releasing artifacts; include license information with released artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative evaluation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When collecting new datasets or making decisions about which datasets to use, authors should assess and communicate the degree to which their datasets are representative of their intended population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of diverse or universal representation should be substantiated by concrete evidence or examples; authors should explicitly describe dataset representativeness and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent communication of societal impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should transparently communicate the known or anticipated consequences of research: for instance via the paper checklist or a separate section in a submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an explicit discussion (or checklist entry) describing potential beneficial and harmful consequences and known limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors should consider whether there are foreseeable situations in which their technology can be used to harm, injure or kill people through its direct application, side effects, or potential misuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not submit research whose primary goal is to increase the lethality of weapons systems; discuss foreseeable harms and mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should consider whether there is a risk that applications could open security vulnerabilities or cause serious accidents when deployed in real world environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If security risks exist, take concrete steps to recommend or implement protections; follow responsible disclosure if reporting vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should consider whether the technology they developed can be used to discriminate, exclude, or otherwise negatively impact people, including impacts on the provision of services such as healthcare, education or access to credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and report potential discriminatory effects; evaluate model behavior across protected groups and document limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should consult on local laws or legislation before collecting or analyzing any bulk surveillance data. Surveillance should not be used to predict protected categories, or be used in any way to endanger individual well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using bulk surveillance data without legal review; do not build or evaluate systems that predict protected attributes from surveillance data or otherwise endanger people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deception and harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should communicate about whether their approach could be used to facilitate deceptive interactions that would cause harm such as theft, fraud, or harassment, and whether it could be used to impersonate public figures and influence political processes, or as a tool to promote hate speech or abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly discuss risks of deception/impersonation or enabling harassment, and consider release controls or mitigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should consider whether their research is going to negatively impact the environment by, e.g., promoting fossil fuel extraction, increasing societal consumption or producing substantial amounts of greenhouse gasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and consider carbon/energy costs and environmental externalities; discuss trade-offs and mitigation strategies where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human rights
rubrics_metrics.description: We prohibit circulation of any research work that builds upon or facilitates illegal activity, and we strongly discourage any work that could be used to deny people rights to privacy, speech, health, liberty, security, legal personhood, or freedom of conscience or religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid research that facilitates human-rights violations; ensure compliance with human-rights considerations and provide justification where risks might arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors should consider any suspected biases or limitations to the scope of performance of models or the contents of datasets and inspect these to ascertain whether they encode, contain or exacerbate bias against people of a certain gender, race, sexuality, or other protected characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and report bias/fairness evaluations, datasets' demographic coverage, and steps taken to mitigate disparate impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and model documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset or the model as part of their submissions via structured templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use model cards, datasheets, or other structured templates to document provenance, collection methods, limitations, intended uses, and known risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and model licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: If releasing data or models, authors should also provide licenses for them. These should include the intended use and limitations of these artifacts, in order to prevent misuse or inappropriate use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach clear licenses that specify permitted uses and restrictions; consider behavioral-use or other restrictive licenses when risk of misuse is high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure and privacy-preserving storage and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should leverage privacy protocols, encryption and anonymization to reduce the risk of data leakage or theft. Stronger measures should be employed for more sensitive data (e.g., biometric or medical data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt appropriate technical safeguards (encryption, access controls, anonymization) scaled to data sensitivity; document protections used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible release and publication strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, e.g. by requiring that users adhere to a code of conduct to access the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider staged releases, access controls, user agreements, or other mitigations; follow responsible disclosure for reported vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing access to research artifacts for scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: When releasing research artifacts, it is important to make accessible the information required to understand these artifacts (e.g. the code, execution environment versions, weights, and hyperparameters of systems) to enable external scrutiny and auditing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient artifact metadata (environments, seeds, hyperparameters, weights) to enable audits and verification where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose essential elements for reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any work submitted to NeurIPS should be accompanied by the information sufficient for the reproduction of results described. This can include the code, data, model weights, and/or a description of the computational resources needed to train the proposed model or validate the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include code, data or descriptions, and computational-cost information sufficient for others to reproduce results; where full release is not possible, explain constraints and provide partial reproducibility materials if feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure legal compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure adequate awareness of regional legal requirements. This can be done, for instance, by consulting with law school clinics specializing in intellectual property and technology issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult legal experts where necessary; provide additional information when legal compliance could not be met due to human-rights considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations reporting and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations to the Code of Ethics should be reported to hotline@neurips.cc. NeurIPS reserves the right to reject the presentation of scientific works that violate the Code of Ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report suspected violations via the designated hotline; note that contributors must also adhere to additional ethical codes or review requirements from funders and institutions.
